evidence.title: Changes in psychiatric documentation and treatment in primary care with artificial intelligence scribe use
evidence.outcome: Likelihood of psychiatric intervention (referral, new diagnosis, antidepressant) in ambient-scribed vs unscribed visits
evidence.effect: Psychiatric intervention was less likely with ambient scribes than with no scribe (aOR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.95). Human scribes showed no difference (aOR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87-1.17). Documented symptoms were greater in ambient-scribed notes.
evidence.quote: In a logistic regression model, likelihood of a psychiatric intervention (referral, new diagnosis, or antidepressant prescription) was significantly lower among ambient-scribed visits compared to unscribed (aOR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.95), but not for human-scribed compared to unscribed (aOR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87-1.17).

commentary.bottom_line: Two deployment studies that tracked outcome and balancing measures after AI rollout report favorable results, but neither compares monitoring with no monitoring, so evidence that this practice prevents downstream harm is indirect. Three hazard studies show that unintended effects on care quality and clinician workload occur and can be measured with outcome proxies.

perspectives.view: The two supporting studies are a quasi-experimental sepsis alert evaluation (n=4517 alerts) and an uncontrolled pre-post study. Both measured outcomes after deployment, yet neither isolates monitoring as the intervention being tested. Observational designs and indirectness each lower certainty, and the panel rates it very low.

In the sepsis study, median alert-to-antibiotic time fell from 140.4 to 112.1 minutes, and a balancing measure found no antibiotic delay. Hazard studies suggest harms may go unseen without surveillance, including lower odds of psychiatric intervention with ambient scribes (aOR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.95) and declining counseling quality in an RCT of 51 patients.

A study of 40 clinicians found NASA Task Load Index scores rose from 43 to 57 after AI deployment, which suggests workload can move opposite to intent. A neonatal pre-post study tracked balancing measures such as ventilator days (10.8 to 7.0) as proxies. Neither study reports the staff time needed to run the monitoring.

None of the five supplied studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The ambient scribe study shows AI can shift clinical decisions, and monitoring that does not report results by payer or language group would be unable to detect whether such shifts differ across populations.

In the ambient scribe study, notes documented more symptoms, yet psychiatric intervention was less likely, while human scribes showed no difference (aOR 1.01). This suggests a tool may record a patient's concern without the concern being acted on. None of the supplied studies reports collecting feedback from patients as part of monitoring.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares a structured post-deployment monitoring program with usual oversight to test whether monitoring detects harms earlier or leads to corrective action. Studies are also needed on which outcome proxies and end-user engagement methods detect safety and workflow signals, and at what staff cost.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the studies testing the practice or documenting the hazard reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether monitoring detects harms in their patients and may need to stratify monitoring results by payer, language, and literacy to find out.
